The effect of missed or delayed PK samples around Tmax on NCA PK parameters

Jerry Hu

2026-08-18

← PK/PD Home Page

1 Summary

Background. Real blood-sampling schedules deviate from plan. A sample near the peak can be missed, or drawn later than planned. The objective is to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule.

Methods. Simulation, NCA, tables and figures, and the statistical analysis were all conducted in R. Concentration–time data were simulated from three one-compartment oral pharmacokinetic models with differing absorption and elimination rates, from 0 to 24 h after a single oral dose (20 subjects per model). The time of peak was held fixed, so the three profiles differ only in peak shape, from a flat plateau to a sharp peak. Four sampling schedules were applied to the same subjects: a near-continuous Dense schedule (one sample per minute), an Intact 13-sample schedule, an Omission schedule with the near-peak sample dropped, and a Delay schedule with that sample drawn 10 minutes late. NCA derived Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf from each schedule. Each deviating schedule was then compared with the intact schedule in the same subjects, as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval on the log scale, and the spread of the individual ratios was summarised.

Results. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across shapes (most in the sharply peaked profile), while it moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2%. A delayed sample, analysed at its actual draw time, changed Cmax by −4.2% to +1.6% and both AUCs by about 1% or less. Individual subjects deviated more than the mean: the lowest single-subject Cmax ratio after a missed sample was 74.7% of intact. Across both deviations the largest change was in Cmax; a single missed or delayed near-peak sample moved NCA exposure only slightly on average.

2 Background

Blood-sampling schedules in clinical pharmacokinetics are finite and planned in advance. The non-compartmental (NCA) parameters they yield — Cmax, Tmax, and the areas under the curve (AUC) — feed exposure and labelling decisions. Unplanned deviations disturb those schedules: a sample is missed, or a sample is drawn late. The peak region is where this should matter most, because that is where the concentration is changing fastest and where Cmax and Tmax are defined.

Objective. Quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule.

3 Methods

3.1 Simulation

3.1.1 Simulation model

The data were simulated with the R package mrgsolve (seed 20260525). The structural model is one compartment with first-order oral absorption: a dosing compartment (GUT) feeds a central compartment (CENT), parameterised by absorption rate ka, clearance CL, and volume V. The model is shown below as both a diagram and equations.

One-compartment model with first-order oral absorption. Dose enters the GUT compartment, is absorbed into CENT at rate ka, and is cleared from CENT at rate CL/V.

\[ \frac{dA_{\mathrm{GUT}}}{dt} = -k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}}, \qquad \frac{dA_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{dt} = k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}} - \frac{CL}{V}\,A_{\mathrm{CENT}}, \qquad C = \frac{A_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{V}. \]

where \(A_{\mathrm{GUT}}\) is the amount of drug in the absorption (gut) compartment, \(A_{\mathrm{CENT}}\) the amount in the central compartment, \(k_a\) the first-order absorption rate constant, \(CL\) the clearance, \(V\) the central volume of distribution, and \(C\) the plasma concentration (\(C = A_{\mathrm{CENT}}/V\)).

The model is defined in mrgsolve. The $OMEGA and $SIGMA blocks carry the between-subject and residual variability described below:

# --- truth model ----------------------------------------------------
# OMEGA = log(1 + CV^2) for 30% log-normal CV ≈ 0.0862 (variance scale).
# SIGMA = (0.10)^2 = 0.01 for 10% proportional RUV (variance scale).
.model_code <- '
$PARAM
TVKA = 5.2, TVCL = 25, TVV = 50

$CMT GUT CENT

$OMEGA @labels ETA_KA ETA_CL ETA_V
0.0862 0.0862 0.0862

$SIGMA @labels PROP
0.01

$PK
double KA = TVKA * exp(ETA_KA);
double CL = TVCL * exp(ETA_CL);
double V  = TVV  * exp(ETA_V);

$ODE
dxdt_GUT  = -KA * GUT;
dxdt_CENT =  KA * GUT - (CL/V) * CENT;

$ERROR
double IPRED = CENT / V;
double DV = IPRED * (1 + PROP);

$CAPTURE IPRED DV KA CL V
'

mod <- mrgsolve::mcode("oral_1cmt_truth", .model_code, quiet = TRUE)

Between-subject variability is log-normal on ka, CL and V (30% coefficient of variation each). Residual error is proportional (10%). Three scenarios share V = 50 L and hold the time of peak at about 0.5 h, differing only in how fast the drug is eliminated relative to how fast it is absorbed. The scenarios are named for the shape of the resulting peak: for this model the curvature of the peak, relative to Cmax, is proportional to ka × kel, so the Plateau profile (ka × kel ≈ 0.9) rises fast and then barely declines, while the Peaked profile (ka × kel ≈ 3.6) has the sharpest peak.

The three profile shapes. Tmax is held near 0.5 h across all three, so the deviating sample lands in the same place each time.
Scenario ka (1/h) CL (L/h) V (L) kel (1/h) t1/2 (h) Tmax (h) Shape
Plateau 9.1 5 50 0.1 6.93 0.5 Fast rise to a flat plateau; slow decline
Moderate 5.2 25 50 0.5 1.39 0.5 Moderate peak and decline
Peaked 3.3 55 50 1.1 0.63 0.5 Sharp peak; fast decline

Each scenario has 20 subjects. The three scenarios share the same dose, sample size and sampling times, and are simulated at one-minute resolution, from which each sampling schedule is then selected:

# V = 50 L throughout; CL chosen so kel = CL/V matches each scenario.
# All three give Tmax in [0.495, 0.505] h via ln(ka/kel)/(ka-kel).
scenario_params <- list(
  plateau  = list(TVKA = 9.1, TVCL = 0.1 * 50, TVV = 50),
  moderate = list(TVKA = 5.2, TVCL = 0.5 * 50, TVV = 50),
  peaked   = list(TVKA = 3.3, TVCL = 1.1 * 50, TVV = 50)
)

# --- study design -----------------------------------------------
N_SUBJ        <- 20
DOSE_MG       <- 100
NOMINAL_TIMES <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)
DELAY_TIME    <- 0.5 + 10/60                       # 10-min delay → 0.6667 h
DENSE_GRID    <- seq(0, 24, by = 1/60)             # 1-min resolution

# --- simulate -------------------------------------------------------
simulate_scenario <- function(scenario_name, pars) {
  mod_s <- param(mod, pars)
  events <- expand.ev(ID = seq_len(N_SUBJ), amt = DOSE_MG, cmt = 1)
  all_times <- sort(unique(c(DENSE_GRID, NOMINAL_TIMES, DELAY_TIME)))

  sim <- mod_s |>
    data_set(events) |>
    mrgsim(end = 24, add = all_times, obsonly = TRUE) |>
    as.data.frame()

  # ODE solver can return tiny negatives at late times when true concentration
  # is ~machine epsilon (peaked scenario, t > ~10 h). Set to zero.
  sim$IPRED <- pmax(sim$IPRED, 0)
  sim$DV    <- pmax(sim$DV,    0)
  sim$SCENARIO <- scenario_name
  sim
}

3.1.2 Sampling schedules

Four sampling schedules are applied to the same per-subject time-courses, so each subject acts as its own control across schedules:

The four sampling schedules. The Dense schedule is re-simulated from the same model, seed, and per-subject random effects, so all comparisons are within-subject.
Schedule Samples (0-24 h) Sampling times (h) Purpose
Dense 1441 0 to 24, every minute Near-continuous comparator (context only)
Intact 13 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 Reference schedule
Omission 12 Intact times with the 0.5 h sample dropped Missed near-Tmax sample
Delay 13 Intact times, but the 0.5 h sample drawn at 0.667 h (+10 min) Delayed near-Tmax sample

The Intact 13-sample schedule is the reference. The Omission and Delay schedules each alter the single 0.5 h near-peak sample. The Dense per-minute schedule is a near-continuous comparator, included only for context: it shows how a practical schedule compares with sampling every minute.

The three practical schedules are built from the same simulated time-courses by selecting times: Omission drops the 0.5 h sample, and Delay replaces it with the draw at 0.667 h:

# --- sampling schedules -----------------------------------------------------
intact <- scenarios_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, NOMINAL_TIMES)) |>
  transmute(SCENARIO, ID, ARM = "intact",
            TIME_NOMINAL = round(time, 6),
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

omission <- intact |>
  filter(!near(TIME_NOMINAL, 0.5)) |>
  mutate(ARM = "omission")

delayed_sample <- scenarios_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, DELAY_TIME)) |>
  transmute(SCENARIO, ID, ARM = "delay",
            TIME_NOMINAL = 0.5,
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

delay <- bind_rows(
  intact |> filter(!near(TIME_NOMINAL, 0.5)) |> mutate(ARM = "delay"),
  delayed_sample
) |> arrange(SCENARIO, ID, TIME_ACTUAL)

obs <- bind_rows(intact, omission, delay)

3.2 NCA

NCA is performed with the R package PKNCA, over the 0–last and 0–inf intervals, using the linear-up / log-down trapezoidal rule for the AUC. The reported parameters are Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf (primary) and Tmax (secondary). Dose-normalised parameters (CL/F, V/F) are not needed for a within-subject comparison and are not reported. The same NCA settings are applied to every schedule, at the actual sample times:

# NCA interval: 0 to infinity. lambda.z is requested because aucinf.obs needs it.
NCA_INTERVAL <- data.frame(
  start      = 0,
  end        = Inf,
  cmax       = TRUE,
  tmax       = TRUE,
  auclast    = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  lambda.z   = TRUE
)

# Parameters reported: Cmax, Tmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf.
NCA_PARAMS_WIDE <- c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "aucinf.obs")

#' Run NCA on one sampling schedule across all (SCENARIO, ID), at the actual sample times.
#'
#' @param obs       Long observation data (SCENARIO, ID, ARM, TIME_*, CONC).
#' @param schedule Schedule to subset ("intact", "omission", "delay").
#' @param run_label Label tagged onto the output (e.g. "INTACT").
#' @return Long PKNCA result with RUN_LABEL attached.
run_nca_schedule <- function(obs, schedule, run_label) {
  stopifnot(schedule %in% unique(obs$ARM))

  sub <- obs %>%
    filter(ARM == schedule) %>%
    transmute(SCENARIO, ID, TIME = TIME_ACTUAL, CONC) %>%
    arrange(SCENARIO, ID, TIME)

  conc_obj <- PKNCAconc(sub, CONC ~ TIME | SCENARIO + ID)
  dose_df <- sub %>% distinct(SCENARIO, ID) %>% mutate(TIME = 0, DOSE = 1)
  dose_obj <- PKNCAdose(dose_df, DOSE ~ TIME | SCENARIO + ID)

  pk_res <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = NCA_INTERVAL))
  out <- as.data.frame(pk_res$result)
  out$RUN_LABEL <- run_label
  out
}

3.3 Statistical analysis

The analysis was pre-specified. All comparisons are paired by subject.

For each of the three ratio parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf), the per-subject ratio of the deviating schedule to the intact schedule is computed on the log scale and summarised as the geometric mean ratio, GMR = exp(mean of the per-subject log-ratios). Each GMR is reported with a 90% confidence interval from the paired t-distribution on the log scale; 100% denotes no effect. The spread of the individual ratios is summarised as the within-subject CV of the ratio (from the SD of the log-ratios), the 5th–95th percentiles, and the minimum and maximum.

Tmax is summarised descriptively, as the median within-subject shift in hours, because it can only take one of the scheduled sampling times.

The estimator takes the per-subject log-ratios, averages them, and back-transforms the mean and its paired-t interval to the ratio scale:

#' GMR + 90% CI for the ratio parameters (paired log-scale estimator).
#' @return per (SCENARIO, parameter, contrast): n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi.
gmr_summary <- function(pairs) {
  pairs %>%
    filter(parameter %in% PARAMS_RATIO,
           is.finite(theta_test), is.finite(theta_ref),
           theta_test > 0, theta_ref > 0) %>%
    group_by(SCENARIO, parameter, contrast) %>%
    summarise(
      n            = n(),
      mean_logdiff = mean(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      sd_logdiff   = sd(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      se        = sd_logdiff / sqrt(n),
      tcrit     = qt(0.95, n - 1),          # 90% CI
      gmr       = exp(mean_logdiff),
      ci_lo     = exp(mean_logdiff - tcrit * se),
      ci_hi     = exp(mean_logdiff + tcrit * se)
    ) %>%
    select(scenario = SCENARIO, parameter, contrast,
           n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi)
}

4 Results

4.1 Simulation

The Dense schedule traces the underlying concentration-time course at one-minute resolution. Across the three shapes the time of peak is held near 0.5 h, so each profile differs only in how sharply it rises and falls.

Mean concentration-time profile under dense (per-minute) sampling for each scenario (Plateau, Moderate, Peaked), semi-log. The time of peak is held near 0.5 h, so the shapes differ only in peak sharpness and decline.

Zooming on the peak over the first 4 h shows how the practical schedules sample it. The Omission and Delay schedules each alter the single 0.5 h near-peak sample, so any divergence between schedules is most visible there.

4.3 Statistical analysis

4.3.1 Geometric mean ratios

Geometric mean ratio (deviating ÷ reference schedule) with 90% CI, by parameter, scenario and comparison. 100% denotes no effect; the Intact-vs-Dense comparison is context only.

The forest plot and table report each geometric mean ratio with its 90% CI, by parameter and scenario. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across the three shapes (geometric mean ratio 92.32%-97.38%), most in the Peaked profile, and moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2%. A delayed sample, analysed at its actual draw time, changed Cmax by −4.2% to +1.6% (geometric mean ratio 95.79%-101.59%) and both AUCs by about 1% or less.

These ratios span several parameters and scenarios and are read as ranges describing magnitude, not as multiplicity-controlled tests.

The Intact-vs-Dense comparison is context, not a further deviation: the intact 13-sample schedule gives a Cmax of 86.41%-88.07% of the per-minute Dense value. This gap is not evidence that the intact schedule misses the true peak — the peak time is 0.5 h by design and 0.5 h is a scheduled sample. It arises because the Dense value is the largest of 1441 observations, each carrying 10% proportional residual error, so the observed dense maximum is inflated relative to the true peak. The intact and dense schedules see the same underlying curve; the difference is in how many chances the residual error gets to push a value above the true maximum.

For Cmax after a missed near-peak sample, the within-subject CV of the ratio was 5.2-8.6% and the lowest single-subject ratio was 74.7% of intact (5th percentile 82.47%-89.22% across scenarios). After a delayed sample the single-subject Cmax ratios ranged from 74.7% to 121.5% — the widest individual spread of any comparison, because a sample 10 min later can fall on either side of a noisy peak. The AUC ratios were far tighter: no individual AUC0-t or AUC0-inf ratio fell below 92.5% or above 102.7%.

4.4 Results Summary

The objective was to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule. Across the three profile shapes:

Effect on Cmax.

  • Omission vs Intact: Cmax was 92.32%-97.38% of intact (lower by 2.6-7.7%) — the largest effect of either deviation, because dropping the near-peak sample widens the gap between the sampled maximum and the true peak; the sharper the peak, the larger the loss.
  • Delay vs Intact: Cmax was 95.79%-101.59% of intact (a change of −4.2% to +1.6%); the sample drawn 10 min late still lands near the peak, and on the Plateau profile can even exceed the 0.5 h value.
  • Individual subjects: the single-subject Cmax ratio fell as low as 74.7% after a missed sample, and ranged from 74.7% to 121.5% after a delayed one.

Effect on AUC (AUC0-t and AUC0-inf).

  • Both deviations moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2% relative to intact on average, and no individual subject’s AUC ratio fell outside 92.5%–102.7%; one near-peak point is a small part of the exposure integral.

Effect on Tmax.

  • Omission moved the recorded median Tmax to the next scheduled time point, since the 0.5 h sample is absent; Delay recorded the actual +10 min draw time. The largest median Tmax shift across the two deviations was 10 min.

5 Discussion

We simulated single-dose concentration–time data from three one-compartment oral PK models spanning slow to fast elimination — and, as a result, a flat plateau to a sharp peak — applied four sampling schedules to the same subjects, derived the NCA parameters from each, and compared each deviating schedule with the intact schedule as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval.

  • Cmax. A missed near-peak sample produced the largest change, lowering Cmax by 2.6-7.7% on average; a sample drawn 10 min late changed it by −4.2% to +1.6%. The loss grows with peak sharpness, so it is the Peaked (fast-elimination) profile that is most exposed. These ratios are relative to the intact practical schedule, not to the true peak, and they assume the deviation falls on the near-Tmax sample; a deviation elsewhere on the curve would affect Cmax less. The delay result also assumes the actual draw time is recorded and used in the analysis; a delayed sample analysed at its nominal time would behave differently and was not studied here.
  • Individual subjects. The mean effect understates what can happen to one subject: the lowest single-subject Cmax ratio after a missed sample was 74.7% of intact. For a study-level GMR a single deviating subject contributes only its share of the mean, but for a single-subject data query or an outlier assessment the individual ratio is the relevant quantity.
  • AUC. AUC0-t and AUC0-inf moved by under 2% under either deviation, because a single near-peak point is a small fraction of the integral. This would not hold for deviations during the absorption phase or for several missing points.
  • Tmax. Omission shifts the recorded Tmax to the next scheduled time point and Delay records the later draw time, so Tmax tracks the sampling times directly. Tmax is the time of the largest observed concentration and is sensitive to residual noise: even the per-minute Dense schedule has an upward-biased median Tmax (0.65 h for the Plateau scenario, versus the 0.5 h design value), because on a flat, slowly-declining peak the largest noisy concentration tends to fall on a later time point. Observed Tmax should therefore be read as approximate.
  • The observed dense-sampling maximum exceeds the 13-sample Cmax. The intact schedule gives 86.41%-88.07% of the per-minute Dense Cmax. Because the peak time is a scheduled sample by design, this gap is not a measure of how far the intact schedule misses the true peak; it reflects the maximum of 1441 noisy observations exceeding the maximum of 13. It is shown for context and should not be read as a bias of the intact schedule.

Other limitations.

  • A single delay magnitude (+10 min on the 0.5 h sample), a single missed sample, and 20 subjects per scenario were studied. Larger delays, multiple deviations, deviations at later time points, and a coarser schedule around the peak (the intact schedule samples every 15 min from 0.25 to 1 h, denser than many Phase 1 designs) would give different numbers.
  • No lower limit of quantification was applied, so late samples in the Peaked scenario that would be below the limit in a real assay still contribute to AUC0-inf.
  • The reference is the intact practical schedule, not model truth, so the Cmax comparisons are “deviating vs intact practical schedule”, not “vs the true peak”.
